Brussel Sprout
Kimchi
Fermentation
If you think you know Brussels sprouts,
prepare to meet them in a completely new
way. Most of us grew up with a big
“ewwwww!” when it came to brussel
sprouts. Usually they were boiled to death
and could only be resuscitated with
slatherings of butter and blizzards of salt.
This fermented Brussel Sprout Kimchi recipe
takes everything people love about classic
kimchi—its tang, heat and Gzz, —and pairs it
with one of the most unexpectedly perfect
vegetables for fermentation. Brussels sprout
kimchi holds its crunch beautifully, soaks up
Iavor like sponges, and develops an almost
nutty sweetness as it ferments.
If you love bold, probiotic-rich Iavors—or
you just want a low-eLort way to level up
your meals—this Brussels Sprout Kimchi is
about to become your new favorite
condiment.
With fermenting, especially in the kimchi
style, brussel sprouts can again be a
delectable taste treat, and a very healthy
one to boot (and don’t worry, this one won’t
make you “boot”).
I Grst made this as a playful twist on
traditional cabbage kimchi, but it quickly
became something I love. It’s quick to prep,
ferments reliably, and is one of those foods
that makes people say, “Oooh yah, dat’s
good!” In fact, I gave a dear neighbor of mine
a taste of this Brussel Sprout Kimchi ferment
straight from the crock and before she left
she asked four times: “Just one more, OK?”
I’ve been making this Brussel Sprout Kimchi
recipe for a long time now and Gnd it to be
quite forgiving. As long as your vegetables
stay submerged and your fermentation
crock, jar or mason jar stays clean, nature
does the rest.
As members of the brassica family, Brussels
sprouts are naturally rich in powerful
compounds like sulforaphane—renowned
for its potential anticancer properties—and
indole-3-carbinol, which supports DNA
repair and may help inhibit the growth of
harmful cells. With this kimchi, you get all
the nutritional advantages of raw Brussels
sprouts plus the probiotic beneGts of
fermentation. A double win for Iavor and
wellness.
During the fermenting process, these little
green gems can soften just enough to
become pleasantly tender while still
retaining a satisfying bite. Their bold, tangy
Iavor makes them an unexpected yet
irresistible treat.
Brussel Sprout Kimchi
yield: 2 QUARTS prep time: 30 MINUTES
additional time: 3 SECONDS
total time: 30 MINUTES 3 SECONDS
Recipe for making Brussel Sprout kimchi.
5.0 Stars (1 Review)
Print
Ingredients
2 1/2 lbs brussel sprouts
1 medium daikon radish
1 1/2 tablespoons diced ginger
1 tablespoon diced garlic
4 tablespoons Korean red pepper
powder
1 tablespoon Gsh sauce or shrimp sauce
(I excluded this)
Brine
2 tablespoons sea salt
4 cups water
Instructions
A. Rinse and gently clean the brussel
sprouts, daikon, and ginger
B. Slice the brussel sprouts in half
lengthwise
C. Cut the daikon into disks approx ⅛"
thick. If your diakon is particularly
fat then cut lengthwise in half or
quarters Grst
D. Dissolve the sea salt in the water to
make a brine
E. Place the brussel sprouts and
diakon in the brine and leave for a
few hours or overnight if you prefer.
Do your best to compress the
veggies to keep them under the
brine if possible.
F. Drain the brine and reserve it for
later
G. Finely dice the ginger and garlic
H. In a large bowl, combine the garlic
and ginger with the drained veggies
and korean chili powder and toss
(this is where you would also add
Gsh sauce or shrimp sauce if you
wish)
I. Place everything in a fermentation
crock, 2 one quart mason jars or a
wide mouth glass jar. Put some
pressure on the ingredients with
your Gst or a pickle packer (I love
these by the way!). Unlike shredded
cabbage ferments, there will likely
not be enough natural liquid
released to fully cover the brussel
sprouts.
J. Place a weight on top of the veggies
to keep them compacted them and
encourage the brine level to rise
above them. In this image I used a
large clear glass jar for the
fermentation so you can see inside
the fermentation vessel.
K. Add back as much of the reserved
brine as necessary until the brussel
sprouts are fully covered while
compacted. In the method pictured
I simply used a plastic bag Glled with
brine to act as a weight. If using this
method, leave the air out of the bag
so it can conform to the shape of
your container. You can of course
use a fermentation crock with a
weight or a mason jars using
weights and an airlock cap.
L. Cover with lid or airlock cap
M. Let this sit and ferment for 2-4
weeks. You can let it go longer if you
wish. Just taste every once in awhile
to see how the Iavor and texture
changes.
N. When the taste is as you like it, jar it
up and refrigerate to signiGcantly
slow the fermentation process.
O. Enjoy!!!!
© fermenTed
CUISINE: Korean / CATEGORY: Recipes
Learn More
Serving Suggestions
Add some to rice bowls, make quirky korean
tacos with them, or eat it straight from the
jar when no one’s looking (my usual). Serve
them as a vibrant hors d’oeuvre, a refreshing
side dish, or simply enjoy them straight from
the jar.
For a festive touch, try piling them high in
the center of a platter of roasted beets—the
colors and Iavors can make a stunning
holiday presentation.
This recipe is a real gourmet treat!
Enjoy!

Reply ↓
fermenTed on October 6, 2013 at 7:59 am said:
Hey Tom. Good questions. I would deGnitely
top oL the green beans. Oxygen is generally
your enemy in fermenting, so keeping your
beans under the brine in this case would be a
very good idea. Not sure of your technique,
but for things like this, I often use a mason
jar and Gll it completely to the top with brine
and then loosely screw on the top so that
gasses and excess liquid can escape.
As to storing ferments, I honestly can’t
answer that as I’ve been refrigerating mine
once done, but I’ll share my thoughts. The
point is that fermentation will continue in
earnest unless you cool it down signiGcantly
at some point, in which case it will simply
slow down. I can’t speak for ALL ferments,
but most can go a long time before needing
refrigeration. As sugar/starch supplies
dwindle in the fermenting item, or as the
chemistry gradually changes in the ferment
itself, you’ll naturally get a die oL of some
bacteria, which is Gne, but it will cause some
discoloration. Most ferments will simply get
more and more sour, but I believe the more
sour they get, the less they will need
refrigeration for preservation as well. Root
cellars were built in the days before
refrigeration for a good reason as cool
temperatures help to preserve foods, and
prohibit active fermentation. Let us know
what you learn as you continue with your
fermentations.

Reply ↓
fermenTed on October 6, 2014 at 9:05 am said:
Fermentations keep well when the
fermentation process is allowed to
continue. Be sure to keep the liquid level
above the veggies, keep mold out, and
keep it in a cooler place. No guarantees,
but mushiness is usually caused by some
other invader. Perhaps your salt level isn’t
high enough…?

fermenTed on January 6, 2017 at 9:08 pm said:
That’s a great question Seth, and
unfortunately it’s one I don’t have an
answer for. At Grst I was confused since
your question is placed on the brussel
sprouts comment board. It took me a
couple of re-readings to recognize that
you were talking about fermenting
sprouted seeds. I personally haven’t run
across fermented seed sprouts nor have I
tried it myself. I honestly don’t see why
they wouldn’t work or be delicious. I think
you might be right about needing to add a
culture, since sprouts are home made
from seeds, they perhaps haven’t had time
or opportunity to cultivate a bacterial
content (no soil contact) so the ferment
may not spring to life in earnest. What I’d
do if I were to try it, would be to simple
throw in a couple of red radishes, or a
cabbage leaf or two, just to inncoulate the
ferment. I tend to not add juice from
previous sauerkrauts since the bacteria
that thrive in fully fermented sauerkraut
aren’t ones that would necesarily thrive in
the less acidic early stage ferment like a
sprout ferment.
good luck if you try and please write back
if you do. Thanks!

eden on January 10, 2017 at 5:13 pm said:
hi Ted
I am very happy I have found your site
(already shared it with few of my friends)…I
have a question: what is the purpose of
soaking the brussel sprouts; is it necessary?
I have added also a bit of dill just to add a
twist…my mom told me to freeze them a bit
so they lose the bitterness
thanks
Reply ↓
fermenTed on January 15, 2017 at 11:20 am
said:
Soaking the brussel sprouts in a brine is a
traditional method for making kimchi.
Since brussel sprouts won’t compact quite
as well under pressure, it’s a little trickier
to get the water level to rise above the
brussel sprouts if you simply salt them
and compress them. Soaking them in
brine gets them a little wetter and also
allows the salt to still start to break down
the cell walls to release more liquid.
Mixing the brine also gives you extra liquid
to add back in if necessary to cover.
Thanks and good luck!
Reply ↓
Maureen on February 12, 2017 at 2:55 pm said:
Dumb question- when Gnished fermenting
and transferring to smaller containers, does
it still need to be in lots of liquid? Can it be
without any liquid?
Reply ↓
fermenTed on February 13, 2017 at 9:20 pm
said:
Never a dumb question. Thanks for asking.
It’s best to keep your ferments in the
liquid from the original fermentation.
They’ll keep pretty well without being
covered, largely because they’ve become
more acidic (lower pH), which keeps them
relatively immune to problems. Mold and
yeasts can grow wherever food and
oxygen meet, so to ensure safer longer
term storage, keep your ferments
submerged or close to it.
